prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not correct hyponatremia faster than 8-10 mEq/L per 24 h — osmotic demyelination risk.
Do not anchor on ammonia 95 µmol/L being only moderately elevated; ammonia correlates poorly with HE grade.
required_recommendations: Lactulose titrated orally to 2-4 soft stools/day (typical start 30-45 mL TID); first-line treatment.
Rifaximin 550 mg PO BID as adjunct (especially given recurrence risk).
IV potassium repletion to correct hypokalemia — hypokalemia drives renal ammoniagenesis and is a classic HE precipitant.
Empiric IV thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose-containing fluids — borderline thiamine 68 nmol/L warrants prophylaxis.
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP in any cirrhotic with ascites + AMS.
Slow sodium correction (≤8-10 mEq/L per 24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) — precipitated by hypokalemia (K 3.2 from diuretics), constipation (5 days), and likely diuretic non-adherence; concurrent hyponatremia is contributory but not primary.

differential.key_features: Na 128 mEq/L — contributory but not severe enough alone (typically <120) to fully account for grade II HE; correct slowly while addressing HE.
Diagnostic paracentesis required to exclude (ascites present); follow-up PMN 82 ultimately rules out.
Thiamine borderline low; no ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus on exam, no MRI periaqueductal signal; give empiric IV thiamine before any dextrose regardless.
EEG shows generalized slowing with atypical triphasic-like waves but no electrographic seizures; benzodiazepine challenge negative on follow-up cEEG.
Platelets 88, INR 1.8 raise risk; CT head excludes hemorrhage.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Hypokalemia promotes renal ammoniagenesis by increasing glutamine extraction in the proximal tubule — an under-recognized but very common HE precipitant.
EEG triphasic waves are non-specific (any metabolic encephalopathy); their absence does not rule out HE, and atypical morphology should not deflect the diagnosis but warrants NCSE exclusion.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Na 128 is contributory; HE remains primary given ammonia 95 with cirrhosis, hypokalemia, constipation, and characteristic exam (asterixis). Correct sodium slowly; treat HE.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose hyponatremic encephalopathy as primary and pursue aggressive sodium correction.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Classic triphasic waves are not required for HE; atypical morphology is common in moderate HE. Pursue benzodiazepine challenge / continuous EEG to exclude NCSE rather than abandoning the HE diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss HE because EEG is not 'classic'.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. V. is a 52-year-old man with NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for 2 days of worsening confusion, difficulty finding words, and increasing irritability. He had been increasingly forgetful over the prior month but the acute worsening began 48 hours ago. His wife noted he could not remember conversations from hours before, was not tracking time, and had been sleeping more than usual during the day while being restless at night — a reversal of his normal sleep pattern. He did not report dark stools, hematemesis, or abdominal pain. His wife reported that he had been constipated for approximately 5 days and had not been taking his spironolactone regularly due to dizziness when standing. He denied alcohol use and urine toxicology confirmed no recent use. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal distension and decreased appetite over the prior week. He had no prior episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. He denied fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia. He had no focal weakness or sensory changes. His medications were reviewed and no new medications had been added.
